clue.text: Showing foresight, stay busy to get rid of a cold

parts.note: a prop is a support or stay

indicators.note: to get rid of something is to throw it out, so a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a hectic day is a busy one
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Advice to a sensible person: keep active and you will shake off your cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay' reads as 'remain', but here it is a noun, a support; 'a cold' removes just one of two identical letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophetic remark predicts what will happen, which is exactly what foresight means.

clue.text: Panda, originally arboreal, sadly an endangered species

indicators.note: what comes originally comes at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the animal's name

indicators.note: something sadly done is done badly, so the letters are knocked out of their order

parts.note: the eight letters of this word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wildlife note: the tree-dwelling panda is, sadly, under threat of extinction.
explanation.walkthrough: The panda and its trees are a decoy; the answer is a different bear, made from P plus a rearrangement of ARBOREAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic's white bear is listed as a threatened animal because melting sea ice destroys its hunting grounds.

clue.text: Boundless universe with short relative assimilation process

indicators.note: without bounds means without edges, so the first and last letters are removed

parts.note: the cosmos is the universe
sis is the shortened form of sister

explanation.surface: A cosmic image: an infinite universe paired with a brief kinsman, apparently absorbing things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boundless' here removes both edges of the word, not just one end.
explanation.definitionFit: Osmosis is the gradual absorption of fluid through a membrane, and figuratively the unconscious taking-in of ideas.

clue.text: Scottish woman attached to railway unit

parts.note: hen is a Scottish form of address for a woman
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A Scotswoman employed by or assigned to a section of the railways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit' looks like part of the railway picture, but it is the definition, a scientific unit.
explanation.definitionFit: The henry is the SI unit of electrical inductance, named after the physicist Joseph Henry.

clue.text: Considered unfinished article nothing unusual

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: the definite article
ought is an uncommon variant of aught or nought, meaning zero

explanation.surface: A critic judged a half-completed piece of writing to be quite ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing unusual' reads as 'ordinary', but it means an unusual word for nothing: OUGHT, a rare spelling of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are past forms describing having weighed something in the mind, as in 'a well-considered plan'.

clue.text: North American people's plates showing signs of ageing

parts.note: the Crow are a Native American people of Montana
plates of meat is Cockney rhyming slang for feet

explanation.surface: Dinner plates of some American community are worn and old-looking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plates' comes from Cockney rhyming slang, where plates of meat stands for feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Crow's-feet are the fine wrinkles fanning from the outer corners of the eyes as people grow older.

clue.text: Drunk as well as teetotal, so abandoned

parts.note: intoxicated by drink or drugs is the sense here
and means as well as
a dry person drinks no alcohol

explanation.surface: Someone both drunk and sober at once ends up deserted by friends.
explanation.walkthrough: The contradiction of drunk and teetotal is the joke; each word just supplies one part of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a ship stranded on shore, and so anyone left stranded without help.

clue.text: Precarious organisation has, of course, new department introduced

indicators.note: what is introduced is brought in, so one letter goes among the others
making something new means remaking it, so the letters take a fresh order

parts.note: the letters of these three words, read as written
D is the abbreviation for department

explanation.surface: A shaky company has, naturally enough, set up a new department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as a casual aside, but its letters, with those of 'has' and a D, are the material rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A structure of balanced playing cards collapses at a touch, so the phrase describes any scheme liable to fall apart.

clue.text: Shield fell over — offending soldier placed here

parts.note: to shield is to guard

indicators.note: a thing knocked over is turned upside down, which in a down entry reads backwards

parts.note: a fell is upland moor, in northern English usage

explanation.surface: A soldier's shield fell over, and the culprit was detained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like the past tense of fall but is a noun, a hill or moor in the Lake District sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A guardroom serves as the military lock-up where soldiers under arrest are held.

clue.text: Dance passion, sergeant?

parts.note: a flame is an ardent passion
a sergeant is a non-commissioned officer, NCO

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the army sergeant has a passion for dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: A sergeant is the usual example of an NCO, the abbreviation for non-commissioned officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamenco is the fiery Spanish folk style of dancing from Andalusia.

clue.text: Visual colour mixing ring replaced by one

indicators.note: mixing stirs things together, so the letters lose their order
one thing replaced by another is swapped out, so a letter is exchanged

parts.note: taken as written
O is ring-shaped
a means one

explanation.surface: An artist blending paints, swapping a ring of one shade for another.
explanation.walkthrough: One of COLOUR's two Os becomes A before the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocular means relating to the eye or sight, the adjective for anything seen.

clue.text: Very cold — about forty seconds to get inside

indicators.note: getting inside means entering, so one letter goes into the others
about means around and about, so the letters are turned around in their order

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: It is so cold you have about forty seconds to get indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About forty' sounds like an approximate number, but 'about' signals that FORTY's letters are rearranged with S among them.
explanation.definitionFit: Frosty weather is below freezing, so it is a natural synonym for bitterly chilly.

clue.text: Out-of-date date? Take care

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old-fashioned expression for dating one person regularly
second meaning: an instruction to proceed cautiously

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out-of-date' suggests expired food, but it describes the phrase itself, dated slang for courting.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a steady relationship was once called this, and the same words urge someone to proceed carefully.

clue.text: Given a lift, Australian is hugged by Ruby?

indicators.note: something hugged is held in someone's arms, so these letters sit inside the other word

parts.note: ruby is a shade of red
A is the abbreviation for Australian
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Australian hitchhiker is picked up and embraced by a woman called Ruby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruby' is capitalised to look like a name, but it is the colour; the question mark admits it is only an example of red.
explanation.definitionFit: To be raised is to be lifted up, so the past participle matches a phrase meaning hoisted.

clue.text: Nobles had to be trained for fair

indicators.note: training something reshapes it, so these letters are formed into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Aristocrats had to be coached before appearing at a fete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' looks like a noun, an outdoor fete, but it is the adjective for pale hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash-blonde hair is a very pale greyish blond, and fair is the general word for light-coloured hair.

clue.text: One acting without love — male for instance, a pessimist

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so these letters surround the rest

parts.note: a doer is one who acts
love is zero in tennis scoring, written O
M is the abbreviation for male
say introduces an example, like for instance

explanation.surface: An actor playing a loveless male part, for example, is a gloomy sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it carries its older meaning of outside, so the actor wraps around everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: A doomsayer constantly predicts disaster, the habit of someone who always expects the worst.

clue.text: Lime, say, ornamental button for tiny jumper

parts.note: the lime, or linden, is an example of a tree
a frog is a decorative toggle fastening on a coat

explanation.surface: A lime-green decorative button sewn on a toddler's knitted sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a sweater, which the surface uses; the definition means something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Tree frogs are small amphibians that leap between branches, so they are literally little jumpers.

clue.text: Space programme at first offers venue for prospective buyers

indicators.note: placed at first means put in front, so the second word named comes before the first

parts.note: a show is a television programme
room means space, as in room to move

explanation.surface: A space programme, in its early stages, invites possible investors to look around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space programme' reads as a NASA project; the two words are separate pieces, and 'at first' sends the second one to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Car dealers and furniture sellers display goods in a showroom so that customers can inspect them before purchasing.

clue.text: Stranger's bust wired (about to get uplift)

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an uplift raises things, and in a down entry reading upwards means reading backwards

parts.note: re means about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A stranger's broken underwired bra needs a lifting fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stranger's' stands for 'stranger is'; 'bust' and 'uplift' play on lingerie but are the two operation signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are comparative adjectives describing something more odd or unusual than another.

clue.text: Essential to have one good horse

parts.note: a must is something essential
an means one
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Advice to a rider: it is vital to own a decent mount.
explanation.walkthrough: The three pieces simply follow one another in clue order, with 'to have' only joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustang is a wild or feral horse of the American plains, a specific breed of equine.

clue.text: CRAFT CAPSIZED BY COUGAR — POWER LOST SHOCK!

indicators.note: a capsized boat is turned over, so the letters are turned backwards

parts.note: art is a craft or skill

indicators.note: what is lost is gone, so a letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: the puma is another name for the cougar
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline: boat overturned by big cat, electricity cut, what a scare!
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals mimic a newspaper headline; 'CRAFT' looks like a boat but is skill, ART, and a cougar is also called a puma.
explanation.definitionFit: Trauma is severe emotional distress following a disturbing event, the psychological sense of a jolt.

clue.text: Star American pioneering scientist

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery

explanation.surface: An American scientist who led the way becomes a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: The scientist is Joseph Lister, the British surgeon who introduced antiseptic methods in the 1860s.
explanation.definitionFit: An A-lister belongs to the top tier of celebrities, the famous names that invitation lists put first.

clue.text: Mince pies still not tempting at first …

indicators.note: to mince is to chop finely, so the letters are cut up and rearranged
not means without, so this letter is removed from the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: at first points to the opening of a word, so only its initial is meant

parts.note: the initial of this word, which is taken away

explanation.surface: Mince pies still aren't appealing to begin with, and the speaker trails off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the three dots ending the clue itself, the punctuation mark it names; 'Mince' looks like the filling but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The three dots are the punctuation mark showing an omission or a sentence left trailing, which is called this.

clue.text: Richard's coastal features?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: belonging to the singer Cliff Richard, by his first name
second meaning: steep rock faces along the shore

explanation.walkthrough: Cliff Richard is a veteran British pop singer, so 'Richard's' is his first name in possessive form; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep rock faces where land meets sea are geographic seaside landforms, such as those at Dover.

clue.text: See 6
On-air bloomer often seen on Bake Off

indicators.note: something on air is broadcast and heard by listeners, so the word counts by its sound

parts.note: a bloomer is something that blooms, a plant in blossom

explanation.surface: A gaffe made live on television is a familiar sight on the baking show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' suggests a blunder, or a British loaf of bread, but it is a plant that blooms. Bake Off is a British television baking contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground wheat powder is the basic ingredient of cakes and bread, so it appears in every episode of the baking contest.

clue.text: See 6
Hospital quota for oxygen supply?

parts.note: A&E, accident and emergency, is the hospital casualty department
a ration is a fixed allowance or quota

explanation.surface: A hospital allocating its limited oxygen to patients.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital emergency department; the ampersand drops out of the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeration means introducing air into something, and the question mark admits air is more than oxygen.

clue.text: See 1 Down
Satire — grr, awful, that's official!

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so these letters are messed up

parts.note: the nine letters of these words, dash ignored

explanation.surface: A grumbling verdict that a piece of satire is terrible, stated with finality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Official' looks like an adjective confirming the verdict, but it is the noun, a person in an office.
explanation.definitionFit: A registrar is a public functionary who records births, marriages and deaths, or a university administrator.
